newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey to raise pension age to cut deficit.
newsitem.headline: Turkey to raise pension age to cut deficit.

text.p: Turkey plans to raise its minimum retirement age to reduce the cost of pensions which are adding to huge public deficits.

But labour unions criticised the plan as "retirement in the grave", saying that life expectancy in Turkey is 10 years less than in most European countries and workers would not live to collect their delayed pensions.

A Labour Ministry official said on Monday that a draft law, passed to the prime minister's office on Sunday, included plans to raise the minimum retirement age, improve health care for pensioners and end illegal working conditions.
Labour Minister Necati Celik said in a statement the the new law would save about 129 trillion lira ($13.9 billion) a year. The government has predicted a 1,300-trillion lira budget defict in 1996.

The law will gradually phase in a minimum retirement age of 55 for men and 50 for women. At present men can retire after working 25 years, with some stopping work as young as 43. Women can retire after 20 years, which means some can stop work at 38.
Labour unions criticised the draft law and an official of the largest trade union confederation Turk-Is said, "This can be called retirement in the grave."
The law also plans a more effective inspection at work places owned by small and medium-sized business and industries, where illegal and under-age employment is very common.

The present pension system was seen as unsustainable by the International Labour Organisation, International Monetary Fund and the World Bank which all have said a reform in the social security system was desperately needed to reduce losses incurred by the three pension institutions in Turkey.
An IMF team will arrive in Turkey next week to discuss the performance of Turkey's ailing economy, including the social security reforms, ahead of a possible new stand-by credit arrangement.
